summary: For ages 7-9: children discover that volcanoes and earthquakes are not scattered randomly but cluster in bands, especially the horseshoe-shaped Ring of Fire around the Pacific Ocean rim. The central learning move is DATA → PATTERN: given many plotted volcano and earthquake locations, the child notices they trace lines rather than spreading evenly, then locates and names the Ring of Fire on a world map. The lesson stops at describing THAT a pattern exists (seeding the later 'why' of plate tectonics), rather than explaining the full mechanism. Success = describe the clustering in bands, locate the Ring of Fire, and state the positions are not random.
misconceptions: Volcanoes and earthquakes happen randomly, anywhere, with equal chance (they cluster in belts).
They only happen where THIS child lives, or never happen anywhere (hazard is geographically concentrated, not uniform).
The Ring of Fire is a single line or an actual ring of fire/lava (it is a zone of many volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific).
All volcanoes/earthquakes are on the Ring of Fire (it is the most active belt, but not the only one).
The pattern is a coincidence (it reflects underlying plate boundaries — the cause taught next).

activities.title: Predict, then reveal: the volcano and earthquake data map
steps: Before seeing any data, mark on a blank world map where you think volcanoes and earthquakes happen — make your best guesses anywhere you like.
Reveal many real plotted volcano and earthquake points and compare them with your guesses.
Trace with your finger the biggest band of dots and describe the shape it makes around the Pacific Ocean.
Point to an area with almost no dots (a 'quiet interior') and an area packed with them (a hazard belt).
Name and trace the Ring of Fire as a horseshoe around the Pacific rim, and find at least one other belt (e.g. along southern Europe into Asia) so the pattern is not reduced to a single ring.
State in your own words whether your friend who said hazards are 'scattered randomly all over the Earth' is right or wrong, and why.
activities.insight: Volcanoes and earthquakes are geographically concentrated in bands, not uniformly spread or randomly placed; the Ring of Fire around the Pacific is the most active of these belts, and the pattern can be read directly from map data.

activities.title: Count the dots: making non-randomness quantitative
steps: Using the plotted map, count or estimate how many dots sit on a belt versus how many sit in the middle of a large plate or ocean interior.
Say what a map would look like if hazards were spread fairly evenly across the whole Earth with no large systematic empty regions.
Compare that even-spread picture with the real data and decide which one matches.
activities.insight: The clustering is strong enough to measure: far more hazard points fall on belts than in the quiet interiors, which is what 'not random' means here.

activities.title: The globe check: the ring wraps the ocean
steps: Look at the same hazard points on a rotatable globe (or a real globe), not just a flat map.
Rotate it to follow the Ring of Fire around the edges of the Pacific basin: from New Zealand up past Asia and Japan, across to Alaska, and down the coasts of the Americas.

Describe how the belt curves around most of the ocean in a horseshoe shape that is open at the southern end, and how a flat map centred on the Atlantic can split it into two separate lines at the map's edges.
activities.insight: The Ring of Fire is one continuous horseshoe-shaped belt around most of the Pacific basin, open towards the south. A flat map, especially one centred on the Atlantic, can split it across the map's edges, while a globe shows it as one connected curve around the ocean.

activities.title: The plate-edge teaser (hand-off, not explanation)
steps: After seeing the hazard belts, overlay or lay the outlines of Earth's giant plates onto the dots.
Notice how most of the dots line up along the plate edges / seams, with only a few away from them.
Say what new question this raises for a future lesson (why do hazards sit on the edges of plates?).
activities.insight: Most hazard belts sit along the edges of Earth's giant plates (a few volcanoes, such as Hawaii, are far from any edge). This is a clue that there is an underlying cause, to be explained in later plate-tectonics topics.

activities.title: Check and sort: reading the pattern
steps: Trace the path of the Ring of Fire on a Pacific-centred map.
Answer: are earthquakes spread evenly across the Earth, or clustered? Explain your choice.
Sort a set of given locations into 'on a hazard belt' versus 'quiet interior'.
Judge a claim: 'They could happen anywhere — they're just scattered randomly.' Is it right, and how do you know from the dots?
Reason about whether knowing this pattern helps you say where the next eruption or big earthquake is MORE LIKELY (on a belt), while being clear the pattern shows likelihood, not certainty.
activities.insight: Being able to locate the Ring of Fire AND judge the 'random' claim from the data shows true understanding, beyond just recalling the name; the pattern also makes some places more likely than others for future hazards.

checkQuestion: Here's a world map with every volcano and big earthquake marked as a dot. A friend says, 'They could happen anywhere — they're just scattered randomly all over the Earth.' Looking at the dots, is your friend right? What do you notice, and what does it tell you?
checkAnswer: The friend is wrong. The dots aren't scattered randomly — they line up in bands, especially a huge ring around the edge of the Pacific Ocean (the Ring of Fire). That pattern tells us volcanoes and earthquakes happen in particular zones (the edges of Earth's plates), not just anywhere.
